outcome: No source dated after 26 January 2024 shows that the (a,-1) Lucas-Wieferich primes are infinite, or finite, for any a; the question stays open for every a, and the in-window items I found concern neighbouring families (base-b Wieferich monogenicity, Carlitz and Drinfeld-module Wieferich primes, Mersenne radical defects, Collatz-peak heuristics) and do not move it.
problem_asks: Reading adopted: for each fixed integer a > 0, separately, is the set of Lucas-Wieferich primes for the pair (a,-1) infinite? Such a prime is an odd prime p not dividing 2QD, with Q = -1 and D = a^2+4, such that U_(p-e)(a,-1) is congruent to 0 mod p^2, where e is the Legendre symbol (D/p) and U_n(a,-1) is the Lucas sequence with U_0 = 0, U_1 = 1, U_n = a*U_(n-1) + U_(n-2). Parts: (1) the infinitude claim for every a > 0; (2) the named instance a = 1, the Fibonacci-Wieferich (Wall-Sun-Sun) primes, of which none are known; (3) the named instance a = 2, the Pell-Wieferich primes, of which 13, 31 and 1546463 are known. The statement asks for infinitude, not an explicit list, a count or a bound. I read 'for any given a' as a claim for each a; a result for infinitely many a, or one conditional on abc, would be a different question. Derived identity (my reduction from sources in events 4, 7, 14 and 16): for odd p not dividing a^2+4 the condition is the same as the a-Wall-Sun-Sun condition, p^2 | F_a(p-((a^2+4)/p)), so the family equals the a-Wall-Sun-Sun primes up to the excluded primes p = 2 and p dividing a^2+4.

events.what_happened: Richard J. McIntosh and Eric L. Roettger, 'A search for Fibonacci-Wieferich and Wolstenholme primes', Mathematics of Computation 76 (2007), 2087-2094. The search reports no Fibonacci-Wieferich prime (Wall-Sun-Sun prime, the a = 1 case) below 2 x 10^14. OEIS A001220 cites the same paper (p. 2088) for the definition of Lucas-Wieferich primes associated to a pair (P,Q). The AMS page refused the fetch (HTTP 403); the content here comes from the search summary and from the OEIS and Wikipedia entries, not from the paper.
events.delivers: Finite computer search for the a = 1 case only: no Fibonacci-Wieferich prime below 2 x 10^14. Per OEIS, it also gives the Lucas-Wieferich definition that defines this family (not verified in the paper). Says nothing about infinitude.
events.remains: All of problem_asks, for every a including a = 1 and a = 2.

events.what_happened: Andreas-Stephan Elsenhans and Joerg Jahnel, 'The Fibonacci sequence modulo p^2 - an investigation by computer for p < 10^14', arXiv:1006.0824 (submitted 4 June 2010). The abstract page reports that for every prime p < 10^14 the Pisano period mod p^2 differs from the period mod p, so there is no Wall-Sun-Sun prime below 10^14, and kappa(p^n) = kappa(p) p^(n-1) for those primes. Wikipedia's Wall-Sun-Sun article attributes to this paper the statement that a Lucas-Wieferich prime for (P,Q) is 'a Wieferich prime to base Q and a Wall-Sun-Sun prime with discriminant D'. The PDF was unreadable here and the abstract page does not mention Lucas-Wieferich primes, so that attribution is unverified.
events.delivers: Finite search for the a = 1 case only, below 10^14. No content on infinitude.
events.doubts: The Wikipedia sentence about (P,Q) is literally odd for Q = -1. Wieferich-to-base-Q means Q^(p-1) = 1 mod p^2; with Q = -1 this is (-1)^(p-1) = 1, which holds for every odd p, so the literal reading would make every odd prime a Wieferich prime to base -1. That cannot be the intended characterisation, and the sentence is not verified against the paper.
events.direction: Computational, a = 1 only; no direction on infinitude.

events.what_happened: F. G. Dorais and D. Klyve, 'A Wieferich prime search up to 6.7 x 10^15', Journal of Integer Sequences 14 (2011), article 11.9.2. The bound for that search is missing from the extracted text. Wikipedia's Wall-Sun-Sun article gives 9.7 x 10^14, which I could not confirm.
events.delivers: Base-2 Wieferich search below 6.7 x 10^15 (not the (a,-1) family). Fibonacci-Wieferich search (a = 1) bound not confirmed; Wikipedia gives 9.7 x 10^14.

events.what_happened: PrimeGrid's Wall-Sun-Sun search (the a = 1 case) ended in December 2022. The PrimeGrid pages were not reached. OEIS A244801 instead says 'if one exists it is > 4*10^16 (cf. PrimeGrid WSS statistics)'. Wikipedia's Wieferich article gives 2^64 for base-2 Wieferich primes.

events.doubts: Bounds conflict across sources: 2^64 (Wikipedia), greater than 4 x 10^16 (OEIS A244801), and 2.8 x 10^16 (an arXiv summary I could not open). Not resolved.

events.what_happened: Wayne Peng, 'ABC implies there are infinitely many non-Fibonacci-Wieferich primes - an application of abc conjecture over number fields', arXiv:1511.05645 (18 Nov 2015, single version). Defines X-base Fibonacci-Wieferich primes for a finite set X of algebraic numbers. Under the Masser-Oesterle-Szpiro abc conjecture for number fields it shows there are infinitely many non-X-base Fibonacci-Wieferich primes, and proposes a conjecture on the rank of the free part of the group generated by X. A search summary attributes a Journal of Number Theory (2020) version to 'Grell and Peng'; not verified.
events.delivers: Conditional on abc for number fields: infinitely many primes that are not X-base Fibonacci-Wieferich. This is the complement of a generalised family, and says nothing about whether the Wall-Sun-Sun primes, or the (a,-1) Lucas-Wieferich primes, are infinite.
events.direction: Complement set, conditional on abc. Does not address the family.

The 'Rei-AIOS' label is a series name, and the share text says 'Three-party co-authorship per OUKC charter v1.0'; no AI system is named, and the body does not say an AI produced or helped write the paper.

events.what_happened: David Niedbala Giraudin, 'A counterexample to a conjecture of Thakur on Carlitz-Wieferich primes', arXiv:2607.15305 (v1 14 Jul 2026; v2 22 Jul 2026). Gives an explicit irreducible c-Wieferich prime of degree 5 over F_(19^3), contradicting Thakur's conjecture that such primes in odd characteristic have degree divisible by p, and gives a closed form for a factor of [5] and M_5. Carlitz-module setting; no Lucas sequences or Lucas-Wieferich primes. The author's Section 6 says the work was done 'in sustained collaboration with an AI assistant (Claude Opus 4.8, Anthropic)'. The Breakthrough Tracker record says 'No substantive AI role was disclosed in the inspected manuscript'; this conflicts with the v2 text read here.

The author states that 'the strategy for each problem emerged from the dialogue between the two'.
systems.basis_quote: in sustained collaboration with an AI assistant (Claude Opus 4.8, Anthropic), used through its standard paid consumer interface.

disputes.summary: AI role in arXiv 2607.15305 (Giraudin). The authors' v2 Section 6 names Claude Opus 4.8 (Anthropic) as an AI assistant with a described role. The Breakthrough Tracker record says no AI role was disclosed in the inspected manuscript. The tracker may have read an earlier version; not resolved here. This is not an event bearing on the (a,-1) question.

Wall-Sun-Sun search bound. Wikipedia says any WSS prime must exceed 2^64 (PrimeGrid, Dec 2022). OEIS A244801 says if one exists it is greater than 4 x 10^16. A search summary cites an arXiv paper for 2.8 x 10^16 and another for 9.7 x 10^14; neither was confirmed in the text read.
The 2^64 bound was attributed in a search summary to Jones (arXiv 2302.10357). The fetched page of that paper contains no such sentence; the bound's source is Wikipedia's citation of PrimeGrid.

Claimed gaps in Rout's 2019 proof (Lucas non-Wieferich primes in progressions), attributed in search summaries to Anitha, Fathima and Vijayalakshmi (Open Mathematics 2023). Not verified: the arXiv text does not mention Rout, and the publisher and PDF were not readable.

Wikipedia's Wall-Sun-Sun article attributes to Elsenhans and Jahnel (2010) a characterisation of Lucas-Wieferich primes for (P,Q) as 'a Wieferich prime to base Q and a Wall-Sun-Sun prime with discriminant D'. The paper's abstract does not mention Lucas-Wieferich primes, the full text was unreadable here, and the literal reading fails for Q = -1.

Bouazzaoui's p-rationality criterion for K-WSS primes was attributed in a search summary to arXiv 2404.08194 (Benfield-Lippard). The fetched text of that paper does not contain it. The criterion's primary source has not been read.

summary: Nothing since 26 January 2024 settles or moves the question for any a. I found no proof, disproof, or computation of infinitude for any a. Two identifications frame it. OEIS A271782 gives the k-Wall-Sun-Sun test as p^2 dividing F_k(p-((k^2+4)/p)) for primes p > 2 not dividing k^2+4, and OEIS A001220 gives the Lucas-Wieferich test as p^2 dividing U_(p-e) with e = (D/p), D = P^2-4Q, for odd p not dividing 2QD. With (P,Q) = (a,-1) these are the same condition, so the family equals the a-Wall-Sun-Sun primes except for p = 2 and primes dividing a^2+4. The discriminant exception is covered by a secondary report (Harrington-Jones) that no odd prime divisor of a^2+4 is a-WSS, and p = 2 is excluded from the Lucas-Wieferich set by definition. So the Lucas-Wieferich set is the a-WSS set minus at most {2}, and the infinitude question is the infinitude of a-WSS primes. This equivalence is my derivation, and Wikipedia's Wall-Sun-Sun article states the (k,-1) correspondence too. Known data: no WSS prime below 2^64 (PrimeGrid, per Wikipedia; OEIS gives greater than 4 x 10^16); for a = 2, exactly 13, 31 and 1546463 below 10^12 (OEIS and Dobson); the smallest 3-WSS prime is 241 (OEIS A271782, whose k = 11, 34, 42 entries are believed to exceed 10^12 if they exist). The infinitude heuristic is a 1/p probability model (McIntosh-Roettger 2007 per Wikipedia), which Klaska (2007) is reported to challenge; I could not read that paper. Other in-window items concern neighbours: Drinfeld-module and base-b Wieferich work (Caruso-Gazda-Lucas 2024; Lucas 2025; Falk-Harrington-Jones and Jones 2026), a Mersenne defect paper (Laniewski 2026), a trinomial WSS(d) generalisation (Shi et al. 2026), a non-peer-reviewed Collatz-peak heuristic (Fujimoto 2026), and a Carlitz counterexample whose authors credit Claude Opus 4.8 (Giraudin 2026). The Ross-Shen-Cai abstract (Dec 2025) mentions WSS primes, but its PDF was unreadable, so I cannot say whether that is a result. Close calls: (1) whether the Wikipedia (P,Q) sentence attributed to Elsenhans-Jahnel is a real statement; (2) whether Ross-Shen-Cai's WSS link is a theorem; (3) whether Anitha et al. really found gaps in Rout's proof; (4) which Wall-Sun-Sun bound is correct. AI search: 42 searches (below) and several lab, tracker and arXiv AI-related queries found no AI involvement in this question; the AI items found are attached to unrelated events. Tool caveat: WebFetch returns model-processed text, so quotes marked verbatim come from that extraction and should be checked against the source.
competing_reading: A reader might count a = 2 as settled up to 10^12: the three known Pell-Wieferich primes below 10^12 are a finite list found by search. That is a search bound, not finiteness, and the question asks for infinitude. A second reader might take Wikipedia's (P,Q) sentence as a different reduction (to Wieferich primes to base Q plus WSS primes with discriminant D), which would change which known results count. As written it fails for Q = -1, so I did not use it. The strongest case for real movement is the Ross-Shen-Cai (Dec 2025) abstract, which links Lucas-sequence valuations to 'the existence of Wall-Sun-Sun primes'. If its full text proves a statement about the existence of WSS primes it would bear on the a = 1 case, though existence is not infinitude.
what_would_settle_it: For a given a: a proof that infinitely many primes p satisfy U_(p-e)(a,-1) = 0 mod p^2, or a proof that only finitely many do; equivalently, for a = 1 or a = 2, the same for WSS or Pell-Wieferich primes. To confirm the reduction: the full text of Falcon-Plaza 2009 and Elsenhans-Jahnel 2010 (to check whether either defines the Lucas-Wieferich set), and Jones 2302.10357's published version. To settle the gap claim: the Anitha et al. Open Mathematics text and Rout's 2019 PDF. To settle the Ross-Shen-Cai link: its full text. To settle the bound: PrimeGrid's own statistics page. To settle the Carlitz AI conflict: the version history of arXiv 2607.15305 and the tracker's version.

dead_ends: No published result on the infinitude of Lucas-Wieferich primes for any a, in any source dated after 26 Jan 2024; searches for 2024-2026 results on this family returned only reformulations and neighbouring families.

No AI-system involvement found for this problem in 42 searches, including the AI-specific queries (AlphaEvolve, AlphaProof, GPT-5, Claude, DeepMind, OpenAI, Anthropic, Erdos-problem trackers, Tao's blog). The only AI-credited item near this topic is Giraudin 2026, which concerns Carlitz c-Wieferich primes.
